## Learning Objectives

After completing this tutorial, you will be able to:

- Compute the gradient of a trajectory-dependent quantity of interest with
  `TimeIntegrator.gradient`, and verify it against finite differences
- Write down the adjoint recursion a time-stepping scheme solves: a terminal
  condition, a backward sweep, and a sum over the trajectory
- Explain why that sweep runs backward in time, rather than taking it on
  faith --- the reason is that transposing the all-at-once Jacobian turns
  forward substitution into back-substitution
- Say what changes when the scheme changes, and what does not


## One Large State Equation

The goal is a gradient: given a quantity of interest computed from a
trajectory, find its derivative with respect to the parameters, at a cost
that does not grow with how many parameters there are. The answer is a
*backward sweep* over the trajectory, and calling for it takes two lines ---
name a functional, then ask the integrator for the gradient. The rest of this
tutorial explains what that sweep solves and why it runs backward, because a
reader who takes the direction on faith cannot debug it when it goes wrong.

[The Adjoint Method](adjoint_concept.qmd) derived a gradient for an objective
constrained by a state equation $\vc{c}(\vc{u}, \vc{z}) = \vc{0}$, and needed
no time and no PDE to do it. A time-stepping run appears to be a different
kind of object: a loop, running forward, producing a trajectory rather than a
single state.

It is not. Collect every computed state into one long vector

$$
\vc{Y} = (\vc{y}_1, \vc{y}_2, \ldots, \vc{y}_N),
$$ {#eq-stacked-state}

and each step of the scheme becomes one block row of a single algebraic
system. For backward Euler, step $n$ contributes

$$
\vc{R}_n(\vc{y}_n, \vc{y}_{n-1}, \vc{p})
= \mt{M}(\vc{y}_n - \vc{y}_{n-1}) - \Delta t\, f(\vc{y}_n, t_n, \vc{p})
= \vc{0},
$$ {#eq-step-residual}

and stacking all $N$ of them gives $\vc{C}(\vc{Y}, \vc{p}) = \vc{0}$ --- a
state equation of exactly the form the previous tutorial treated, only larger.
Everything derived there applies verbatim. What this tutorial adds is
*structure*: the all-at-once Jacobian is not a dense matrix, and its shape is
what makes the adjoint recognizable as a backward sweep.


## The Shape of the All-at-Once Jacobian

Each step residual @eq-step-residual involves only two states: its own and its
predecessor. So $\partial \vc{R}_n / \partial \vc{y}_m$ vanishes unless
$m = n$ or $m = n-1$, and the Jacobian $\mt{C}_{\vc{Y}}$ is **block lower
bidiagonal**: diagonal blocks $\mt{A}_n = \partial \vc{R}_n/\partial
\vc{y}_n$, and one subdiagonal of blocks $\mt{B} = \partial \vc{R}_n /
\partial \vc{y}_{n-1}$, which for backward Euler is just $-\mt{M}$.

Before reading anything off that shape, one clarification, because
$\vc{C}(\vc{Y}, \vc{p}) = \vc{0}$ is in general **nonlinear**. A matrix is
not the system; $\mt{C}_{\vc{Y}}$ is its Jacobian, evaluated at the converged
trajectory. So the two directions are not the same kind of computation:

**Forward stepping follows the pattern of block forward substitution, but
each block is a nonlinear solve.** The dependency structure is what the lower
bidiagonal shape records --- $\vc{y}_1$ from the initial condition, then
$\vc{y}_2$ from $\vc{y}_1$, down the diagonal --- while the arithmetic inside
each block row is Newton's method, iterating until @eq-step-residual is
satisfied. Nobody substitutes through a nonlinear system.

**The adjoint system genuinely is a linear solve, and back-substitution is
literal.** Once the forward trajectory is known, the adjoint equation of the
previous tutorial reads
$\mt{C}_{\vc{Y}}^\top \boldsymbol{\lambda} = -(\partial Q/\partial
\vc{Y})^\top$ with $\mt{C}_{\vc{Y}}^\top$ a fixed matrix built from the
converged states. Transposing moves the coupling block from below the
diagonal to above it, and an upper triangular system is solved by *back*
substitution --- last unknown first. The backward-in-time adjoint sweep is
not a separate algorithm anyone had to invent; it is what block
back-substitution looks like when the blocks are indexed by time.

That asymmetry is worth keeping in mind: the backward sweep costs **one
linear solve per step** even when the forward solve needed several Newton
iterations at every step. Linearizing once, at the solution, is the whole
economy of the adjoint method.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-all-at-once
#| fig-cap: "The all-at-once Jacobian and its transpose, for four steps. Blue blocks are each step's dependence on its own state, orange its dependence on the previous one. Notice that transposing moves the orange blocks from below the diagonal to above it, and the green arrow reverses: the same substitution algorithm now resolves the last time step first. This is the whole reason adjoint sweeps run backward in time."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pyapprox_tutorials.figures._adjoint import plot_all_at_once_blocks

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 4.4))
plot_all_at_once_blocks(axes)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

This also explains the transpose that the previous tutorial showed to be
load-bearing. Dropping it there produced a plausible but wrong gradient; here
it would mean solving the adjoint system in the wrong direction entirely.

Writing the transposed system out block by block gives the recursion an
implementation follows. With $\mt{A}_n^\top$ on the diagonal and
$\mt{B}^\top$ above it, the last block row involves only
$\boldsymbol{\lambda}_N$, so it is solved first, and each earlier multiplier
follows from the one after it:

$$
\mt{A}_N^\top \boldsymbol{\lambda}_N = -\left(\pd{Q}{\vc{y}_N}\right)^\top,
\qquad
\mt{A}_n^\top \boldsymbol{\lambda}_n
= -\left(\pd{Q}{\vc{y}_n}\right)^\top - \mt{B}^\top \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{n+1},
$$ {#eq-adjoint-recursion}

after which the gradient assembles as a sum over the trajectory,

$$
\nabla_{\vc{p}} Q
= \pd{Q}{\vc{p}}
+ \sum_{n=1}^{N} \boldsymbol{\lambda}_n^\top \pd{\vc{R}_n}{\vc{p}} .
$$ {#eq-transient-gradient}

Those two blocks are not a derivation that lives only on paper. A stepper
exposes them directly: `adjoint_diag_jacobian` returns $\mt{A}_n^\top$ and
`adjoint_off_diag_jacobian` returns $\mt{B}^\top$, and the integrator's
adjoint solve walks the recursion using them.

A different scheme changes what the blocks contain --- Crank-Nicolson and
Heun evaluate $f$ at more than one point, so their diagonal blocks differ ---
but not the bidiagonal shape. That shape follows from each step depending
only on its immediate predecessor, which is true of every scheme PyApprox
provides: all of them are one-step methods. A multistep method, whose update
reaches back several steps, would widen the band and lengthen the recursion
correspondingly, without changing anything else about the argument.


## Computing the Gradient

The forward pipeline is the one from
[Time Stepping for ODEs](ode_timestepping_usage.qmd). The only additions are
a functional saying what scalar to differentiate, and the `Adjoint` tier of
the stepper, which carries the two block accessors named above.

```{python}
import numpy as np

from pyapprox.ode.functionals.endpoint import EndpointFunctional
from pyapprox.ode.implicit_steppers.backward_euler import BackwardEulerAdjoint
from pyapprox.ode.implicit_steppers.integrator import TimeIntegrator
from pyapprox.util.backends.numpy import NumpyBkd
from pyapprox.util.rootfinding.newton import NewtonSolver
from pyapprox_benchmarks.functions.ode.linear_ode import LinearODEResidual

bkd = NumpyBkd()
nstates, nparams = 2, 2

# dy/dt = A y + B p: the parameters enter as a forcing.
residual = LinearODEResidual(
    bkd.asarray(np.array([[-1.0, 0.5], [0.2, -2.0]])),
    bkd.asarray(np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])),
    bkd,
)
integrator = TimeIntegrator(
    0.0, 1.0, 0.1, NewtonSolver(BackwardEulerAdjoint(residual)),
)
# Q reads one state component at the final time.
integrator.set_functional(
    EndpointFunctional(state_idx=0, nstates=nstates, nparams=nparams, bkd=bkd)
)

param = bkd.asarray(np.array([[0.5], [0.3]]))
residual.set_param(bkd.flatten(param))
init_state = bkd.asarray(np.array([1.0, 0.5]))

states, times = integrator.solve(init_state)
gradient = integrator.gradient(states, times, param)
print("trajectory:", states.shape)
print("gradient  :", bkd.to_numpy(gradient).ravel())
```

One backward sweep over the trajectory produced both components. Note what
the call did *not* require: no re-solve per parameter, and no derivative of
the time-stepping loop with respect to anything.

The gradient is the exact derivative of the *computed* quantity of interest
--- the one the scheme actually produced, discretization error and all --- not
an approximation of the derivative of the continuous problem. That is what
makes it usable by an optimizer: the objective and its gradient describe the
same discrete function, so a line search behaves.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Verification

```{python}
#| echo: false
eps = 1e-6
fd_gradient = np.zeros((1, nparams))
for index in range(nparams):
    for sign in (1.0, -1.0):
        perturbed = bkd.copy(param)
        perturbed[index, 0] += sign * eps
        residual.set_param(bkd.flatten(perturbed))
        perturbed_states, _ = integrator.solve(init_state)
        value = bkd.to_float(integrator._functional(perturbed_states, perturbed))
        fd_gradient[0, index] += sign * value / (2 * eps)
residual.set_param(bkd.flatten(param))

adjoint_np = bkd.to_numpy(gradient)
relative = np.linalg.norm(adjoint_np - fd_gradient) / np.linalg.norm(fd_gradient)
print("adjoint          :", adjoint_np.ravel())
print("central difference:", fd_gradient.ravel())
print(f"relative error   : {relative:.2e}")
assert relative < 1e-6, "adjoint gradient disagrees with finite differences"
```

The two agree to the accuracy a central difference can resolve, which is the
same check [the first tutorial](adjoint_concept.qmd#sec-verification) applied
to a static system.
:::


## The Cost Argument, Again

The reason for all of this is the same one as in the static case, and it
survives the extra structure: the adjoint costs one backward sweep whatever
the number of parameters, while finite differences need a fresh forward solve
per parameter.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-cost-vs-nparams
#| fig-cap: "Time to compute one gradient against the number of parameters, log-log. Finite differences rise linearly --- each parameter buys two more forward solves --- while the adjoint stays flat, since the backward sweep is the same size no matter how many parameters the forcing carries. Notice that the timings come from a handful of runs in the documentation build and are correspondingly noisy; the slopes are the claim, not the values."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pyapprox_tutorials.figures._adjoint import (
    measure_gradient_cost,
    plot_gradient_cost_scaling,
)

nparams_list = [2, 4, 8, 16, 32]
adjoint_times, fd_times = measure_gradient_cost(nparams_list)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.2))
plot_gradient_cost_scaling(nparams_list, adjoint_times, fd_times, ax)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

For the two-parameter problem above the difference is not worth discussing.
For a control problem whose parameters are the nodal values of a field, it is
the difference between a gradient that takes one backward sweep and one that
takes thousands of forward solves.

### What Changes for Automatic Differentiation

[The first tutorial](adjoint_concept.qmd) weighed the adjoint against
reverse-mode automatic differentiation and found the deciding issue to be
that AD differentiates the program that ran: taping a Newton solve records
every iteration, so its cost grows with the iteration count while the adjoint
uses only the converged linearization.

Time stepping multiplies that. The tape now grows along two axes at once ---
iterations *within* a step, and steps --- so a run of $N$ steps taking $k$
Newton iterations each records $Nk$ linearizations. Measured on the backward
Euler loop for this problem, the recorded operation count is almost exactly
$21$ per step at three iterations per step ($106$, $211$, $421$, $841$ nodes
at $5$, $10$, $20$, $40$ steps) and rises in proportion to the iteration
count at fixed step count ($71$, $141$, $211$, $351$ nodes at one, two, three
and five iterations). The adjoint sweep is one linear solve per step, whatever
$k$ is.

Memory is the sharper constraint, and it is new here. Reverse mode must
retain everything the backward pass will need: the whole trajectory *and*
every Newton iterate within every step. The adjoint retains the trajectory
alone, and need not even do that --- checkpointing schemes store a subset of
states and recompute the rest during the backward sweep, trading solves for
storage at a ratio the user picks. On a transient PDE with a large state
vector, that difference decides whether the gradient can be computed at all.


## Key Takeaways

- A time-stepping run is one large state equation over the stacked
  trajectory; the adjoint derivation needs no modification to handle it.
- The all-at-once Jacobian is block lower bidiagonal because each step
  couples only to its predecessor.
- Forward stepping is block forward substitution; the transposed system is
  upper bidiagonal, so the adjoint sweep runs backward in time. That is the
  origin of the backward sweep, not a separate algorithm.
- `adjoint_diag_jacobian` and `adjoint_off_diag_jacobian` are the blocks of
  $\mt{C}_{\vc{Y}}^\top$; changing the scheme changes the block contents, not
  the structure.
- The discrete adjoint gives the exact gradient of the computed quantity of
  interest, which is what an optimizer needs.

- [Quantities of Interest Over a Trajectory](transient_functionals_concept.qmd)
  replaces the endpoint functional used here with a time integral, which
  contributes to the backward recursion at every step rather than one --- and
  which must be summed with the quadrature rule the scheme implies.
- *Steering a Plume* (forthcoming) applies this to a PDE-constrained control
  problem, where each block of $\mt{C}_{\vc{Y}}$ is itself a sparse
  finite-element operator and the parameter count makes the cost argument
